items.text: SEASON 7 · EPISODE 7 · DRAFT  Field visit · Maya, Luis, Renske (the site electrician) and Adaeze · Level L5 · Advanced support (formulas on request)  Valmera’s new training centre was fitted from HQ’s central stock. The rack room smells of hot varnish, and every recording has bands rolling through it.  ⚑ RV-154: power is the site electrician’s — nobody touches a hot unit; smoke or flame means the fire alarm. RV-151: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Fifty Hertz
items.stakes: A rack room that smells of hot varnish, and recordings with bands rolling through every lesson. Both came from the standard.

items.reward: A safe rack, clean recordings, and a standard that says where it applies.

items.title: The converter in the rack.
items.body: Renske's findings: HQ's central stock sent the standard UPS — a 120 V-only unit. The local installer, handed a 120 V box in a 230 V building, ran two of them from small 1,000 VA travel converters. Recharging, each UPS drew about 1,400 W: at least 140% of the converter's rating. One scorched. The parts list had no voltage column; ‘standard’ meant ‘standard in Harrowmere’.
items.label: Test: how overloaded were the converters — and whose call is it?

items.alt: A rack power sheet: two red boxes, UPS A and UPS B, both 120 V only and fed through 1,000 VA converters; 1,400 W on 1,000 VA is at least 140%; the parts list has one UPS model for every country; isolated by the site electrician.
items.caption: Standard in Harrowmere. Scorched in Valmera.

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Luis and Maya beside a board. Fifty-hertz mains here. The LED panels pulse a hundred times a second. Your HQ profile shoots at a sixtieth. A sixtieth holds one and two-thirds pulses — the leftover shows as bands. A hundredth holds exactly one. Or we shoot fifty frames, like everyone else in Valmera. Either way it's design, not drift. Write it down.

hints.text: What's the right part — and who installs it?

items.title: Fifty and sixty
items.body: In the 1890s the companies building the first alternating-current systems tried many frequencies. North America settled on 60 Hz; most of Europe, and much of the world after it, on 50 Hz — choices made by competing manufacturers and engineers, not by physics. More than a century later, every camera that crosses between them has to be told which one it's in.

items.text: Act II — “A hundred pulses a second”

items.alt: A training room with the camera's view on the front display: pale horizontal bands rolling down the picture of the presenter. Adaeze points at them; Maya frowns.

bubbles.text: Every recording. Bands, rolling. HQ's camera profile, untouched.

items.prompt: HQ ships us kit for another continent, then calls my fixes ‘drift’.

options.label: “Then the standard's wrong, not Valmera. Let's write the regional variants — voltage, frequency, cameras — and make the scanner read them.”
options.reply: I've waited three years to hear someone from HQ say ‘the standard's wrong’.

options.label: “The installer shouldn't have used converters.”
options.reply: The installer was handed a 120 V box in a 230 V building and told it was standard.

options.label: “Why didn't you flag it?”
options.reply: I did. The ticket was closed as ‘non-standard request’.

items.title: UPS-1500 (all sites)
items.body: The HQ central-stock parts list: ‘UPS-1500 · all sites’. Columns: part number, quantity, price. No voltage. No frequency. No plug. A list written in a 120 V building.

items.title: A hundred pulses a second.
items.body: The LED panels run on Valmera's 50 Hz mains and pulse a hundred times a second. The HQ camera profile — 59.94 frames a second, a 1/60 s shutter — holds one and two-thirds pulses per exposure; the leftover third shows as bands, rolling because the frame rate doesn't divide the pulses evenly. The scanner flags any change to that profile as drift.
items.label: Test: why the bands — and what is a 50 fps profile here?
**Work it out:** stop the bands on Valmera's recordings.

items.prompt: Friday. What should Valmera's cameras be?
unknown: What the change board will say
items.risk: A course launched with unusable recordings — or a fix the scanner calls drift.

hints.text: Which shutter holds a whole number of pulses — and where does that get written down?

options.label: Keep the HQ profile — the standard is the standard
options.result: Every lesson recorded with bands through it.
options.fail: A standard must say where it applies.

options.label: A Valmera regional variant — 50 fps with a 1/100 s shutter (1/100 s at 59.94 for anything HQ must receive at 59.94) — approved by the change board, recorded, and read by the scanner
options.result: Approved Friday afternoon. The scanner turns Valmera's cameras from red to ‘variant · approved’.
options.consequence: Design, recorded where the tools can read it.

options.label: Switch the LED panels off and teach by daylight
options.consequence: Removes the light to fix the camera.

options.label: Fix it in the edit
options.result: Forty hours of lessons a week, each hand-cleaned.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #68 · AVERY'S LENS  A standard must say where it applies  A part number, a camera profile or a setting is only ‘standard’ where its assumptions hold — voltage, frequency, language, law.  The HQ standard UPS was a 120 V part. In Valmera it arrived with a pair of travel converters, and one of them scorched.

items.alt: The rack power sheet after the fix: two green boxes, UPS A and UPS B at 230 V on Circuit 1 at 12.2 A; region-rated, installed and signed by the electrician; the parts list now has voltage, frequency, plug and regional equivalents.
items.caption: The right part, signed by the right person.

items.title: // global
items.body: The camera profile, distributed to every site: ‘59.94 fps · shutter 1/60 · // global’. Correct for Harrowmere's 60 Hz lights. Wrong for Valmera's and Tahvara's 50 Hz ones — and ‘global’ means the scanner flags any change.

items.label: **Service Mode:** run the two days yourself.

items.alt: Monday: the course launches in a lit training room; the front display shows a clean picture of the presenter; Luis and Maya at the back.

bubbles.text: A clean picture, a cool rack, and my cameras aren't red on your scanner any more.
They were never wrong. The standard was.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  A part or setting is only “standard” where its assumptions hold: list voltage, frequency, plug and the regional equivalent. Never improvise power — the fix for the wrong part is the right part, installed and signed by the site electrician; a hot unit is theirs to isolate. Lights on mains pulse at 2 × f mains ; a shutter that holds a whole number of pulses removes the bands. Record regional variants so the scanner reads design as design.
